Glass travels at something like 3000m/s through glass, roughly 350 through air. I could provide a billion other examples to support that generally higher density = higher speed of sound and lower density = lower. So why does sound travel so fast through helium?
Why does sound travel through helium faster than air, when generally higher density = higher speed of sound?

I'm not good at explaining science, but here's my try:

In gas a wave of denser gas advances by moving molecules nearing each other. The molecules try to arrange as far from each other as possible. The bigger the molecules, the bigger the repulsion between them. Mass needs time to accelerate, so this needs some time.

In a solid the molecules can't move much and are much closer. And the force holding them together is stronger than the one forcing them apart. Mass still needs time to accelerate, but the closer the molecules are the stronger the repulsing forces are, so the wave travels faster than through a gas.

Helium doesn't conduct heat as well, that heat adds to the compression wave.

From a value standpoint, air has a Cp/Cv ratio of 1.4. Helium is 1.03.

In case you've read everyone else's comments, but you're still confused:

The major factors involved in the speed of sound are the following:

  1. The molecule's weight.

  2. The average spacing between molecules.

  3. The degrees of freedom of the molecule. (We'll ignore this one because it makes the explanation needlessly complicated, but degrees of freedom just means how many ways a molecule can react when impacted by another molecule speeding in to it (e.g., it can cause it to spin, jiggle, bounce away, etc). The more ways it can react the more degrees of freedom the molecule has.)

Lighter individual molecules means faster sound. Check out this youtube video for an easy visual. Skip to 3:30 to get to the interesting part: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LXUdRGw8UP4
Picture yourself in a large inflatable ball (maybe you weigh 150lbs) and imagine a car (weighing 1,500lbs) that is in its own bubble running into you at 10mph. If the energy is perfectly conserved during the collision then you can get knocked away at up to 100mph (10x faster than the car hit you.) Helium is lighter than air, so to carry the same energy it must move faster.

Your example of glass vs air overlooks a very important difference. Glass is a solid, and air is a gas. The average inter-molecular spacing is vastly different in the two substances. Air's "mean free path" between between collisions is around 70nm. However the "mean free path" in a solid is only slightly larger than its chemical bonding distance (~200pm) since the molecules are packed so closely together. Therefore, a gas molecule has to travel approximately 350 times further (70nm vs 0.2nm) before it can start to impart its speed on its neighbor. To get a good idea why this lack of spacing increases the speed of sound so much, remind yourself of a "Newton's Cradle" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton's_cradle

I probably didn't answer your question exactly, but hopefully you have a better fundamental understanding of the influencing factors.
